movement_source: row 'Net interest margin (%) — Group Performance from continuing operations', column 30 Jun 20 -> column 30 Jun 21
headline: CBA's Group net interest margin declined 4 bps to 2.03% in FY21 from 2.07% in FY20 (cash basis). The decline was driven by higher liquid asset drag (-4 bps), lower asset pricing (-2 bps) from home loan switching and competition, and higher funding costs (-3 bps) from the falling cash rate environment. These were partially offset by favourable portfolio mix (+2 bps) from higher deposit funding ratios and TFF drawdowns, improved basis risk (+3 bps) from bill/OIS spread dynamics, and positive capital/other (-2 bps) from lower capital earnings, plus Treasury & Markets contribution (+2 bps). Ex-liquids, NIM was flat as pressure from lower rates was offset by mix and funding benefits.

drivers.narrative: Decreased margin by 4 basis points driven by increased lower yielding non-lending interest earning assets, including liquid assets (ev-5). Higher deposit funding ratio and at-call deposit balances, plus drawdown of the TFF contributed to elevated liquid asset balances (ev-12).

Decreased margin by 2 basis points driven by lower business lending margins (down 1 bps) from repricing actions to support businesses during COVID-19, and lower consumer finance margins (down 1 bps) from a reduction in the proportion of interest earning credit card balances. Home lending margins were flat, reflecting repricing (up 9 bps), offset by customers switching from variable to fixed rate loans (down 5 bps) and increased competition (down 4 bps) (ev-6).

Decreased margin by 3 basis points, reflecting lower earnings on transaction and savings deposits mainly due to decreases in the cash rate (down 7 bps), partly offset by higher benefits from the replicating portfolio (up 2 bps) and lower wholesale funding costs (up 2 bps) (ev-7).

Decreased margin by 2 basis points driven by lower earnings on Group capital due to the falling interest rate environment (down 3 bps), partly offset by increased contribution from New Zealand (up 1 bps), reflecting lower wholesale funding costs and favourable portfolio mix, partly offset by the impact from RBNZ cash rate cuts (ev-10).

Increased margin by 2 basis points driven by a higher average deposit funding ratio (30 June 2021: 77%; 30 June 2020: 71%) due to strong growth in transaction and savings deposits, customers switching to at-call deposits, and the drawdown of the TFF (up 4 bps), partly offset by an unfavourable impact from asset mix (down 2 bps), mainly due to a decline in higher margin consumer finance balances (ev-8).

Margin increased 3 basis points reflecting a decrease in the average bank bill swap to OIS spread notwithstanding a structural reduction in exposure to basis risk due to strong growth in cash rate linked deposits and a mix shift towards fixed rate home loans (ev-9).
Increased margin by 2 basis points driven by higher bonds and commodities financing income in Global Markets (ev-11).

limitations: The results book provides a narrative decomposition rather than a formal walk chart; the presentation slide provides the visual walk chart. Both are consistent.
The headline NIM figure differs between the Group-level table (2.03%/2.07%, -4 bps) and the RBS divisional table (2.60%/2.63%, -3 bps); we report the Group margin as required by the task.
The 'ex-liquids' framing mentioned on the presentation slide (ev-12) indicates that excluding the liquids drag, NIM was essentially flat, which changes the interpretation of the overall decline.

evidence_records.quote: The Bank's net interest margin decreased 4 basis points on the prior year to 2.03%. The key drivers of the movement were:
Liquid assets: Decreased margin by 4 basis points driven by increased lower yielding non-lending interest earning assets, including liquid assets.

Asset pricing: Decreased margin by 2 basis points driven by lower business lending margins (down 1 basis point) from repricing actions to support businesses during COVID-19, and lower consumer finance margins (down 1 basis point) from a reduction in the proportion of interest earning credit card balances. Home lending margins were flat, reflecting repricing (up 9 basis points), offset by the impact of customers switching from higher margin loans to lower margin loans, particularly from variable rate to fixed rate loans (down 5 basis points) and increased competition (down 4 basis points).

Funding costs: Decreased margin by 3 basis points, reflecting lower earnings on transaction and savings deposits mainly due to decreases in the cash rate (down 7 basis points), partly offset by higher benefits from the replicating portfolio (up 2 basis points) and lower wholesale funding costs (up 2 basis points).

Portfolio mix: Increased margin by 2 basis points driven by a higher average deposit funding ratio (30 June 2021: 77%; 30 June 2020: 71%) due to strong growth in transaction and savings deposits, customers switching to at-call deposits, and the drawdown of the TFF (up 4 basis points), partly offset by an unfavourable impact from asset mix (down 2 basis points), mainly due to a decline in higher margin consumer finance balances.

Basis risk: Basis risk arises from the spread between the 3 month bank bill swap rate and the 3 month overnight index swap rate. The Bank's margin increased 3 basis points reflecting a decrease in the average spread notwithstanding a structural reduction in exposure to basis risk due to strong growth in cash rate linked deposits and a mix shift towards fixed rate home loans.

Capital and other: Decreased margin by 2 basis points driven by lower earnings on Group capital due to the falling interest rate environment (down 3 basis points), partly offset by increased contribution from New Zealand (up 1 basis point), reflecting lower wholesale funding costs and favourable portfolio mix, partly offset by the impact from RBNZ cash rate cuts.
Treasury and Markets: Increased margin by 2 basis points driven by higher bonds and commodities financing income in Global Markets.
